17812: Whitefield's dramatic open-air preaching drew enormous crowds in Britain and America. His central theme was the necessity of the new birth: outward religion and church membership cannot save; each person must be inwardly converted by the Spirit. Itinerants such as Gilbert Tennent warned of the danger of an unconverted ministry.
17813: Preaching shifts toward individual conversion as a datable crisis, addressed to mass audiences across denominational lines, using print and publicity. Historians debate whether a single 'Great Awakening' existed or is partly a later construct (Jon Butler).
17814: Jonathan Edwards: Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God
17816: Preaching on Deuteronomy 32:35, Edwards pictured the unconverted held over the pit of hell only by God's restraining hand, and urged immediate flight to Christ while the door of mercy stood open. Hearers reportedly cried out during the sermon. Elsewhere Edwards preached at length on the beauty of God and Christ, analysed true religious affections, and in his *History of the Work of Redemption* sermons expected the gospel to spread before a glorious future age.
17817: Heaven-or-hell destiny, pressed on the individual conscience for immediate decision, becomes a signature of revival preaching. Scholars caution that this one sermon is not typical of Edwards' corpus, whose centre is God's glory and spiritual beauty.
17818: Charles Finney and the new measures
17821: Finney preached that sinners are able and obligated to change their own hearts and submit to God now. He used 'new measures': protracted meetings, direct personal appeals, praying for people by name, and the anxious seat where the convicted came forward. His *Lectures on Revivals* argued that a revival is not a miracle but the result of the right use of appropriate means. Converts were also directed toward social reform, notably abolition and temperance.
17822: Conversion becomes a public, immediate act of the will that can be invited and counted, the ancestor of the altar call and decision card. Critics (Old School Presbyterians, Nettleton, later historians) saw a shift from God's work to human technique; defenders see a recovery of human responsibility and urgency.
17827: Powerscourt (Ireland), later Britain and North America
17830: At prophecy conferences at Powerscourt (1831–33) and in Brethren circles, Darby developed a scheme distinguishing God's earthly purpose for Israel from his heavenly purpose for the church, with a secret rapture of the church before a future tribulation. The kingdom preached by Jesus was seen as offered to Israel, rejected and postponed. His tours in North America after 1862 spread these ideas among evangelicals.
17831: End-times prophecy becomes a prominent evangelistic theme, and expectation of an any-moment rapture adds urgency to conversion. The origins of the pre-tribulation rapture (Darby's own reading, Irvingite prophecy, Margaret MacDonald's 1830 vision, earlier writers) are disputed.
17833: William Miller and the Great Disappointment
17834: Low Hampton, New York, and the northeastern United States
17837: Miller, a Baptist farmer-preacher, calculated from Daniel 8:14 that Christ would return around 1843, a date later fixed by followers at 22 October 1844. Tens of thousands were urged to prepare for the imminent end through camp meetings and a vigorous press.
17838: When Christ did not appear, the Great Disappointment discredited date-setting for many but gave rise to Adventist movements, including Seventh-day Adventism. It showed how powerfully end-times urgency could drive mass preaching in a postmillennial-leaning culture.
17839: D. L. Moody: urban mass evangelism and the lifeboat
17840: Chicago, and campaigns in Britain and US cities
17844: Moody's campaigns preached the three Rs (ruin by sin, redemption by the blood, regeneration by the Spirit) and God's love, with gospel songs by Sankey and inquiry rooms for seekers. Influenced by premillennialism, he likened the world to a wrecked ship and his task to saving as many as possible in the lifeboat. He also founded schools and a Bible institute.
17845: Premillennial urgency combines with organised urban revivalism. Social reform recedes relative to individual rescue, a change historians link to the later fundamentalist–modernist split and the 'great reversal'.
17849: Under the African American preacher William Seymour, a multiracial mission proclaimed salvation, sanctification and the baptism in the Holy Spirit evidenced by speaking in tongues. Participants understood this as the latter rain before Christ's soon return, empowering missionaries to evangelise the world quickly. Building on Parham's teaching (Topeka, 1901), news spread through the mission's paper *The Apostolic Faith*.
17850: The Holy Spirit's experienced power moves to the centre of the gospel for a movement that became global Pentecostalism and charismatic Christianity. Its interracial character drew both admiration and hostility, and later fractured along racial lines.
17854: Scofield's annotated King James Bible printed dispensational notes beside the text: seven dispensations, a distinction between Israel and the church, a pre-tribulation rapture, and a distinction between the 'gospel of the kingdom' (to Israel, and again in the tribulation) and the 'gospel of the grace of God' preached to the church now.
17855: For millions of English-speaking evangelicals the dispensational framework became simply what the Bible says. The church-age gospel was framed mainly as forgiveness and heaven, while Jesus' kingdom preaching was often assigned to Israel. Revised editions (1917, 1967) and progressive dispensationalists since the 1980s have modified these distinctions.
17857: C. H. Dodd reconstructs the apostolic kerygma
17860: Dodd compared the speeches in Acts with Paul's letters and argued for a common apostolic proclamation: the age of fulfilment has dawned; it has come through the ministry, death and resurrection of Jesus, descended from David; he is exalted as Lord; the Spirit is the sign of his present power; he will return; therefore repent and receive forgiveness and the Spirit.
17861: Biblical scholarship begins to measure later preaching against a reconstructed kerygma that is centred on Jesus' resurrection and lordship more than on individual guilt and afterlife. Critics question how uniform the early preaching was and how far Luke's speeches reflect actual sermons.
17864: Los Angeles (1949), London (1954), New York (1957) and worldwide
17868: Graham's sermons typically diagnosed the modern person's emptiness, guilt and fear of death, presented Christ's death for sin and his resurrection, warned of judgment, and closed with an invitation to come forward and receive Christ as Saviour and Lord. Phrases like 'the Bible says' and 'make your decision' were characteristic, and follow-up teams counselled inquirers. Over time he emphasised God's love, racial integration of his meetings and cooperation with a wide range of churches.
17869: Personal decision for Christ, assured forgiveness and eternal life became the public face of evangelical gospel preaching, carried by radio, film and television. His cooperation with mainline churches (1957) split separatist fundamentalists from the new evangelicals.
17870: Four Spiritual Laws and the sinner's prayer
17871: Los Angeles (UCLA) and Arrowhead Springs, California
17874: Campus Crusade's founder distilled the gospel into four points: God loves you and has a plan for your life; humans are sinful and separated from God; Jesus is God's only provision for sin; we must individually receive Christ by personal invitation, usually through a suggested prayer (often with Rev 3:20). Developed in the 1950s and printed as a booklet in 1965, it was distributed in vast numbers. Similar tools followed (the Bridge illustration, the Romans Road, Evangelism Explosion's diagnostic question about where one would go if one died tonight).
17875: The gospel becomes a portable, reproducible presentation aimed at a moment of personal reception. Supporters credit it with enabling ordinary Christians to share faith; critics argue it reduces the gospel to a transaction about sin and afterlife, separates Saviour from Lord, and leans on a prayer formula without clear New Testament precedent. The history of the sinner's prayer itself (precursors in Finney, Moody and Torrey's inquiry practices) is debated.
17877: George Eldon Ladd: the kingdom already and not yet
17879: Ladd argued, in popular and academic form, that the kingdom of God is God's dynamic reign, already inaugurated in Jesus' ministry, death and resurrection and not yet consummated. Drawing on European scholarship such as Cullmann's *Christ and Time*, he challenged classic dispensationalism's postponed kingdom from within evangelicalism.
17880: Inaugurated eschatology became the dominant evangelical scholarly framework, laying groundwork for later kingdom-centred gospel presentations and for Vineyard-style 'kingdom ministry' of healing (John Wimber drew on Ladd).
17882: Second Vatican Council and Catholic evangelisation
17886: The council described the church as the pilgrim people of God and the seed of the kingdom, affirmed that those who through no fault of their own do not know the gospel may attain salvation, and linked hope for a new earth to human work for justice. Paul VI's *Evangelii Nuntiandi* (1975) defined evangelisation as proclaiming the kingdom and salvation in Christ, including liberation from all that oppresses.
17887: Catholic preaching shifts from a strong emphasis on outside the church no salvation and the four last things toward the kingdom, Christ-centred scripture and social dimensions. Critics debate whether this weakened missionary urgency; supporters see recovery of the biblical breadth of the gospel.
17892: About 2,700 evangelical leaders from some 150 nations adopted the Lausanne Covenant. It defined evangelism as proclaiming the crucified and risen Christ as Saviour and Lord and inviting repentance and faith, while affirming that evangelism and socio-political involvement are both part of Christian duty. Latin American speakers such as Padilla and Escobar pressed for an integral gospel of the kingdom against what they saw as a culturally captive North American message.
17893: Global South voices reshape evangelical understanding of the gospel's scope ('integral mission'). The relative priority of evangelism and social action remained contested, discussed further in later Lausanne documents (Manila 1989, Cape Town 2010).
17895: United Kingdom and North America (Oxford, Durham, Los Angeles)
17898: N. T. Wright argued that Jesus announced Israel's return from exile and God's return to Zion, and that the gospel is the royal announcement that the crucified and risen Jesus is Lord, with resurrection and new creation (not disembodied heaven) as the Christian hope. Dallas Willard criticised 'gospels of sin management' that leave discipleship optional. Precursors include Moltmann's *Theology of Hope* and Newbigin's missional theology.
17899: Many pastors and scholars re-centre preaching on kingdom, resurrection, Lordship and new creation. Critics (e.g. John Piper on justification) argue that this can blur imputed righteousness or the urgency of personal guilt and judgment; Wright replies that he affirms both and is reframing, not denying, them.
17900: The King Jesus gospel and salvation by allegiance
17901: Chicago area and Illinois (Northern Seminary; Quincy University)
17906: Scot McKnight argued that evangelicals had become 'soterians' who equate the gospel with a plan of salvation, while the apostolic gospel (1 Cor 15) is the story of Israel fulfilled in Jesus the Messiah and Lord, from which salvation flows. Matthew Bates proposed that pistis in the gospel context is best understood as embodied allegiance to Jesus the king, so that saving faith includes loyalty, not mere mental assent or a one-time prayer.
17907: The debate over what 'the gospel' is moves into popular church discussion. Reformed critics such as Greg Gilbert (*What Is the Gospel?*, 2010) hold that the gospel's core remains God's holiness, human sin, Christ's substitutionary death and the response of faith, and some reviewers argue Bates risks blurring faith and works. Supporters respond that they are restoring context and scope rather than replacing atonement or grace.
